ety.text: Old Norse kakabor. Middle English cake English cake From Middle English cake, from Old Norse kaka (“cake”) (compare Norwegian kake, Icelandic/Swedish kaka, Danish kage), from Proto-Germanic *kakǭ, of disputed origin. Likely a distant cognate with kaak. Perhaps related to cookie, kuchen, and quiche. Doublet of coca (pastry).

senses.d: A rich, sweet dessert food, typically made of flour, sugar, and eggs and baked in an oven, and often covered in icing.
ex: On Monday afternoon, Ronya attends a birthday party and eats cake whenever cake is presented to her.

senses.d: A small mass of baked dough, especially a thin loaf from unleavened dough.
A thin wafer-shaped mass of fried batter; a griddlecake or pancake.
A block of any various dense materials.
Synonym of buttocks, especially a pair that are exceptionally plump or full.
ex: Since I started doing squats, I've built up some serious cake.

senses.d: A multishot fireworks assembly comprising several tubes, each with a fireworks effect, lit by a single fuse.
Synonym of pie, the whole of a wealth or resource, to be divided into parts.
Coat (something) with a crust of solid material.
ex: His shoes are caked with mud.

senses.d: To form into a cake, or mass.
Of blood or other liquid, to dry out and become hard.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French gasteau, from Old French gastel, from Frankish *wastil, from Proto-Germanic *wastilaz, from Proto-Indo-European *wes- (“to eat; consume”). Compare Old English wist (“food; provision; feast”) and obsolete English wastel, Sicilian guasteḍḍa (“a kind of round bread”).
From Latin turta. Thought to derive from Latin tŏrta f (“twisted”), which yielded tòrta in Italian.

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish biscocho, from Early Medieval Latin biscoctus (literally “twice baked”). Doublet of biscotte and bísquet/bísquete.
Unadapted borrowing from English cake, from Middle English cake, from Old Norse kaka. Doublet of queque.
